profilePeriod: Treasurer 1983–1991 and Prime Minister 1991–1996, with explicitly dated later public statements through September 2026.
scopeNote: Answers are editorial simulations of documented political principles, not a questionnaire completed by the person. Brazil-specific statements are interpreted in the analogous home-country context. Modern hypothetical technologies require inference.

sources.title: National Archives: Paul Keating during office
sources.evidence: Native Title legislation, Working Nation employment support, APEC liberalisation and republican agenda; relations with Suharto continued despite East Timor abuses. Electoral defeat ended his government.

sources.title: Heads of Government communique
sources.evidence: Commonwealth, state and local leaders coordinated transport, electricity, mutual recognition and vocational training; federal cooperation rather than state abolition.

sources.title: An Australian Republic: The Way Forward
sources.evidence: Republic proposal retained representative parliamentary government and required two-thirds parliamentary support for the president, rejecting a competing direct electoral mandate.

sources.title: Human Rights (Sexual Conduct) Act 1994
sources.evidence: Federal legislation protected consensual adult private sexual conduct from arbitrary interference across Commonwealth, states and territories.

sources.title: ANU Press: The perfect storm of gun control, Alpers and Ghazarian
sources.evidence: Keating supported stricter gun import restrictions and nationally coordinated gun control in Safer Australia, while acknowledging state law-and-order responsibilities; national agreement was not achieved during his premiership.

sources.title: The Privacy Imperative in the Information Age Free for All
sources.evidence: Defended enforceable privacy rights against media intrusion, subject to competing public interests and freedom of expression; privacy is not rendered obsolete by technology.

sources.title: NSW Voluntary Assisted Dying Legislation statement
sources.evidence: Welcomed defeat of assisted dying legislation and called for care and support at the end of life.

sources.title: Keating statement on opposition immigration policy
sources.evidence: Defended multicultural policy as a source of fairness and cohesion and opposed an immigration moratorium.

sources.title: Angus Taylor and the Liberal Party moral decline
sources.evidence: Opposed deportation based on cultural values and monocultural nationalism, defended migrant contributions and the democratic two-party tradition.

sources.title: Parliamentary chronology of immigration detention policy
sources.evidence: Keating introduced mandatory detention for designated unauthorised arrivals, then extended it to unlawful non-citizens; this limits any inference of open borders from multiculturalism. Verified in indexed parliamentary text; direct page access restricted.

sources.title: Disturbing admissions from US Republican Congressman
sources.evidence: Rejected joining a US war over Taiwan as contrary to Australian interests; criticised military integration under AUKUS as loss of sovereignty. These are his claims, not independently established assessments of deployments or war outcomes.

sources.title: Commitment of Australian Forces to Somalia
sources.evidence: Announced substantial Australian forces for UN-mandated Operation Restore Hope to protect humanitarian aid; therefore not an absolute noninterventionist.

sources.title: Reserve Bank: Privatisation in Australia
sources.evidence: Records Commonwealth Bank initial tranches, Qantas and CSL privatisation during Labor government; later sale receipts must not all be attributed to Keating.

sources.title: Superannuation Guarantee statement
sources.evidence: Defended compulsory employer contributions to retirement savings, combining regulation and private/industry funds rather than replacing the market with state production.

sources.title: Government CGT Changes: Structurally Sound
sources.evidence: Supported equal treatment of real capital gains and employment income and criticised preferential capital taxation; still argued entrepreneurship responds strongly to opportunity.

sources.title: The Reserve Bank and Monetary Policy
sources.evidence: Criticised monetary tightening and delayed bond purchases for weakening employment; defended an employment-conscious central-bank mandate, not abolition of central banking.

sources.title: Radio 2LM interview
sources.evidence: Identified as Christian, located human dignity in Christian teaching without demanding others follow his faith; supported means-tested pensions and Medicare, lower company tax, innovation, and clear federal/state infrastructure responsibilities.

sources.title: Tenth anniversary of Sex Discrimination Act
sources.evidence: Supported sex equality, affirmative action, childcare and wider employment opportunities for women; rejected confinement of women to traditional roles.

sources.title: Peter Dutton: Climate Denialist, Peddler of Danger
sources.evidence: Strongly opposed nuclear power while backing renewable energy investment and urgent carbon abatement; cannot treat him as embracing every technology.

sources.title: The Compact City: Urban Design and Architecture
sources.evidence: Supported compact urban development and design, treating cities as central to modern civilisation rather than advocating rural retreat.

sources.title: Adelaide press conference
sources.evidence: Promoted cooperative research centres including tissue growth and genetic engineering, arguing that research and education confer technological competitive advantage. Does not establish a position on designer embryos or brain implants.

sources.title: National Archives: Paul Keating after office
sources.evidence: Confirms self-authored Engagement: Australia Faces the Asia-Pacific, published March 2000, explaining his government foreign policy; mentions Japanese and Chinese translations.

sources.title: Google Books bibliographic record: Engagement
sources.evidence: Lists author Paul Keating, Macmillan 2000, original English title, ISBN 0732910196; political and international-relations content.

sources.title: Keating official Australia and the World index
sources.evidence: Latest listed substantive foreign-policy statement is 18 September 2026; society/economy index and dedicated October 2026 search revealed no later substantive change. This is a search bound, not proof of no other statements.

facts: Created COAG cooperation in 1992; retained distinct state responsibilities while promoting national standards.
1994 sexual privacy legislation established nationally applicable rights.
estrutura.tension: National coordination does not amount to abolishing federalism; native title is not a right of state secession.

facts: 1995 republic model placed the president under parliamentary appointment and removal.
Governed through elections and accepted 1996 defeat.
representacao.tension: Strong executive reform leadership and suspicion of competing direct mandates coexist with democratic accountability; no sortition or assembly government.

facts: 2010 defended privacy remedies; 1994 protected adult private sexual conduct.
1995 sought stronger gun restrictions; opposed assisted dying in 2017.
poder.tension: Civil liberties are substantial but coexist with gun control, border detention and protection of life; not a blanket right to all private conduct.

facts: 1992 and April 2026 defended multiculturalism and rejected exclusion by cultural background.
His government enacted mandatory immigration detention.
imigracao.tension: Cultural pluralism does not imply unrestricted border entry; English participation and retention of heritage can coexist.

facts: September 2026 rejected war over Taiwan and military dependence on Washington.
1992 deployed troops under UN mandate to Somalia.
diplomacia.tension: Diplomacy and arms restraint, but national defensive capabilities and selective humanitarian force remain legitimate.

facts: UN intervention in Somalia and regional engagement under his government.
2026 asserted Australian sovereign interests against automatic participation in US conflict.
intervencao.tension: Neither isolationism nor expansionist force; practical cooperation with Suharto complicated universal human-rights principles.

facts: Privatised competitive public businesses including Qantas and CSL; supported Commonwealth Bank sell-downs.
Retained social health provision, targeted pensions and compulsory superannuation.
economia.tension: Market ownership plus social protection differs both from laissez-faire and collective ownership.

facts: Compulsory superannuation, targeted industry research and 2026 capital-gains tax fairness.
2021 sought stronger monetary support for employment.
controle.tension: Liberalised markets coexist with national social regulation and macroeconomic intervention; neither comprehensive planning nor abolition of monetary authority.

facts: Promoted tariff reductions and regional APEC trade liberalisation.
Linked domestic competitiveness to education, innovation and export engagement.
comercio.tension: Active industry capability building did not mean high protective tariff walls.

facts: 1994 explicitly identified Christian human dignity as a moral source, without requiring others to follow him.
2017 opposed assisted dying; 1994 protected sexual privacy.
religiao.tension: Religious ethics and secular equal citizenship coexist; opposition to theocracy is not atheism.

facts: 1994 advocated affirmative action, equal employment and childcare for women; protected consensual adult sexual privacy.
2017 rejected assisted dying on human dignity grounds.
moral.tension: Progressive civic equality does not establish radical permissiveness on every sexual, reproductive or family issue.

facts: 1993 funded research including genetic engineering; 2010 endorsed compact cities.
2024 opposed nuclear power and supported renewables.
tecnologia.tension: Modernisation and science coexist with ethical and environmental limits; specific transhumanist positions are not documented.

uncertainties: Preserved profilePeriod: Treasurer 1983–1991 and Prime Minister 1991–1996, with explicitly dated later public statements through September 2026. Checked official indexes and current searches through 2026-10-01; no later relevant policy change located.
Brazil-specific questions are answered by substantive analogy to Australian institutions, not as claims that Keating commented on Brazilian legislation.

Phone unlocking, facial recognition, cryptocurrency, gender terminology, adoption, abortion and human-enhancement answers are reasoned simulations from documented principles rather than direct quotations or individually verified policy endorsements. D/C express modest inference, not certainty.

Neutral choices mark genuine competing considerations: language versus cultural assimilation, sanctions versus sovereignty, public faith and church charitable status, reproductive/family autonomy versus Christian ethics, nuclear versus other technology and therapeutic versus enhancement biotechnology.

Three independent institutional accounts (National Archives, RBA, ANU research) supplement primary government records and Keating statements. Several archival pages needed search-index or link traversal access; that limitation is stated where used.

Book search included Engagement and After Words, author bibliography, National Archives, Google Books, and Portuguese/Brazilian translation search. No Brazilian translation verified; retain original title instead of inventing one.

bookDecision.reason: Self-authored political account of Asia-Pacific engagement; most directly relevant sustained exposition of his foreign-policy thought. First publication March 2000. No prior catalog book; no Brazilian edition found.

religionMetadataReview.reason: Secular governance or private/cultural faith without the strong public religious identity required for tagging above the threshold; no religion tag inferred from ethnicity.
